newsitem.title: USA: Analysts see Miami budget deal as significant step.
newsitem.headline: Analysts see Miami budget deal as significant step.

text.p: Municipal bond rating agencies and insurers hailed the Florida oversight board's stamp of approval on Miami's five-year budget plan as a significant benchmark.
"This is a very important move away from the brink," said Hy Grossman, managing director for municipal ratings at Standard & Poor's Corp. "We have a financial plan that's substantially credible."
After the oversight board approved the city's five-year budget earlier this week, S&P raised its rating on Miami's general obligation debt to BB from single-B.
Both S&P and Moody's Investors Service cut Miami's GO rating to junk-status after the city disclosed it had a $68 million deficit in its $275 million budget for fiscal 1997.
Moody's did not change its Baa1 rating after the budget was approved but changed its rating outlook to "stable" after the five-year plan was submitted in late April.

"It's a real positive step forward for the city. It really was a large deficit relative to the budget that they had to address in a relatively short period of time. They should get recognition for the fact that they've done that," John Incorvaia, a vice president at Moody's, said.
"It's a plan that appears logical," he said.
The budget agreement and the oversight board's insistence that debt service payments be held in escrow have also eased some of the concern of the firms that insure Miami's bonds.

"We bleieve that Miami has taken the first necessary steps on its way back to fiscal stability. We are particularly comforted by the fact that the state of Florida has taken an active role in helping restore the city's financila health," said Tito Davila, spokesman for Financial Guarantee Insurance Co, which insures about $116 million of Miami debt.

"We are pleased with the actions of the state oversight board and the establishment of a debt service escrow account to ensure timely payments on all bond issues," said Mike Ballinger, a vice president at MBIA Insurance Corp., which insures about $10 million of Miami debt.

The five-year plan relies on a new fire district tax, operating efficiencies and cuts in benefits and services to balance the budget. It also lays out plans for public-private development that is expected to increase property tax revenues.

The rating agencies said the city still faces major hurdles, especially in negotiating new contracts with union workers who accepted deep concessions to help the city balance the 1997 and 1998 budgets. Their contracts expire at the end of 1998.
Miami's finance department is also woefully understaffed and undertrained, and it remains to be seen whether the city can follow through on the five-year plan, the analysts said.
"Obviously we have to make sure the revenues are going to come in and the expenditure cuts are going to be acheived" before the city's investment-grade status can be restored, Incorvaia said.
But for muni traders, Miami's financial decline and subsequent progress has been almost moot.
The city has only about $370 million of general obligation and special obligation debt outstanding, a pittance compared to other cities. All but about $12 million of that is insured.
"We've seen no bonds during this entire six months," Jeff Martin, a muni trader at First Miami Securities Inc, said.
"People don't believe that Miami's going to default on its debt. The insured bonds are not affected and there's just no unsecured debt available. There's nothing to trade," Martin said.
